draft.title: Police powers
card: Police have powers to stop, search, question and arrest people. These powers exist to help them prevent and investigate crime.
Police powers are set by law. In NSW they are mainly found in the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002, often called LEPRA.
Police can use a power only in the situations the law allows. For example, they usually need a reasonable suspicion or belief about a person before they search that person without a warrant.
Police who go beyond their powers act unlawfully. Evidence they gain that way may be challenged in court, and the officers may face consequences.
draft.remember: Police powers are real, but they come from law and have limits.

a.q: Which statement best describes the source of police powers in NSW?
opts: They are set by law, mainly LEPRA, and have limits
They come from police policy, which police can change
They are set by courts case by case, with no statute
They are unlimited when police are investigating crime
a.why: Police powers come from law, mainly the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002. The tempting option about police policy is wrong because police cannot widen their own powers beyond what the law allows.
a.clue: Think about which law the card names.

b.q: Officer Ruiz in Newcastle searches a man's bag without a warrant. She had no reasonable suspicion and no other lawful ground. What is the best description of her action?
opts: It went beyond her powers, so it may be challenged
It was lawful, because police may search anyone
It was lawful, because police do not need grounds to search
It was unlawful only if she found nothing in the bag
b.why: Police can search without a warrant only where the law allows, and usually need reasonable suspicion or another lawful ground. Without one, the search goes beyond her powers. Finding something does not make an unlawful search lawful, and the evidence may still be challenged.
b.clue: Does the card say police can use powers without grounds?

a.best: They are set by law, mainly LEPRA, and have limits

b.best: It went beyond her powers, so it may be challenged

proposal.title: Police powers
card: Police have powers to stop, search, question and arrest people. These powers exist to help them prevent and investigate crime.
Police powers are set by law. In NSW they are mainly found in an Act passed by the NSW Parliament: the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002, often called LEPRA.
Police can use a power only in the situations the law allows. For example, they usually need a reasonable suspicion or belief about a person before they search that person without a warrant.
Police who go beyond their powers act unlawfully. Evidence they gain that way may be challenged in court, and the officers may face consequences.
proposal.remember: Police powers are real, but they come from law and have limits.

a.q: Where do NSW police mainly get their powers to stop, search and arrest?
opts: An Act of Parliament that sets limits on when they apply
Police policy that senior officers can change when needed
Court rulings made case by case, with no Act involved
An officer's own judgement about what each case needs
a.why: NSW police powers come mainly from LEPRA, an Act of the NSW Parliament, which limits when each power can be used. Police policy is tempting, but police cannot widen their own powers beyond what Parliament's law allows.
a.clue: Think about who makes the rules that police must follow.

b.q: Officer Ruiz in Newcastle searches a man's bag without a warrant. She had no reasonable suspicion and no other lawful ground. What is the best description of her action?
opts: It went beyond her powers, so it may be challenged
It was lawful, because she did not arrest the man
It was lawful, because police do not need grounds to search
It was unlawful only if she found nothing in the bag
b.why: Police can search without a warrant only where the law allows, and usually need reasonable suspicion or another lawful ground. Without one, the search goes beyond her powers. Finding something does not make an unlawful search lawful, and the evidence may still be challenged.
b.clue: Does the card say police can use powers without grounds?

a.best: An Act of Parliament that sets limits on when they apply

b.best: It went beyond her powers, so it may be challenged
